covers.quote: Use capitals for proper nouns and genus names
Otherwise don’t use initial capitals for the names of:
diseases and viruses
diagnostic procedures
syndromes
anatomical parts.

Anatomical part named after a proper noun
Syndrome named after a proper noun
Diagnostic procedure in lower case
Anatomical part in lower case

rules.quote: Use an initial capital letter for medical terms only if the term is a proper noun or adjective, or if it is the name of a genus.
rules.violation_condition: a medical term that is not a proper noun, proper adjective, or genus name written with an initial capital letter, or a proper noun/adjective/genus name written without one
when: Do not use initial capitals for the names of diseases and viruses, diagnostic procedures, syndromes, or anatomical parts unless they contain a proper noun, proper adjective, or genus name.
rules.why: G-1 and G-4: The heading is restated and expanded by the body sentence and its list items.

covers.quote: Spell out the full term in lower case, unless the word or term you’re shortening includes a proper name or a genus name.

examples.note: Spelled out term in lower case with uppercase acronym
Genus and species retains capitalised genus name
Spelled out term in lower case with uppercase acronym
Spelled out term in lower case with uppercase initialism
Spelled out term in lower case with uppercase initialism

rules.quote: Use capital letters for acronyms and initialisms of medical terms.
rules.violation_condition: an acronym or initialism of a medical term written in lower case, or its expanded spelled-out term capitalised when not containing a proper name or genus name
when: Spell out the full term in lower case, unless the word or term being shortened includes a proper name or a genus name.
rules.why: G-2: The sentence pairs the acronym rule with the capitalization rule for the spelled-out form.

examples.note: Named after Lou Gehrig, a person who had the disease
Named after members of the American Legion who had the disease

rules.quote: If it is a disease named after people who had the disease, use the possessive case.
rules.violation_condition: a medical eponym for a disease named after a person or group who had the disease written without the possessive case
when: Applies when referring to a disease named after people who had the disease.
rules.why: G-2: Contrast rule to non-possessive eponyms for discoverers.

covers.quote: This rule doesn’t apply to names of organisations dedicated to studying certain diseases or supporting people who are affected by them. Always refer to organisations in the same way as they refer to themselves.

examples.note: Named after Dr Alois Alzheimer, who first described the disease
Named after Dr John L H Down, who first described the syndrome
Anatomical part named after Gustav Jakob Henle
Organisation self-reference exception
Organisation self-reference exception

rules.quote: If it is a disease or anatomical part named after the person who discovered, studied or described it, don’t use the possessive case.
rules.violation_condition: a medical eponym for a disease or anatomical part named after the person who discovered, studied, or described it written in the possessive case
when: Applies to diseases and anatomical parts named after discoverers or researchers.
Does not apply to names of organisations dedicated to studying certain diseases or supporting people affected by them (refer to organisations as they refer to themselves).
rules.why: G-2 and G-3: Absorbs the organisation name exception.

covers.quote: Italicise organism names
Use an initial capital for the name of the genus only.

examples.note: Genus capitalised, species lower case, formatted in italics

rules.quote: Write scientific names of infectious organisms – such as viruses, bacteria and parasites – in italics.
rules.violation_condition: the scientific name of an infectious organism not written in italics, or genus name not capitalised, or species name capitalised
when: Use an initial capital for the name of the genus only; keep the species name in lower case.
rules.why: G-1 and G-4: The heading is restated by the sentence, which also covers genus initial capitalization.

covers.quote: Cite common names for pharmaceutical drugs, not brand names
Write them in lower case.
You can include the brand name in parentheses after the common name. Use initial capitals for brand names.

examples.note: Generic name in lower case followed by brand name in parentheses
Generic name in lower case followed by brand name in parentheses

rules.quote: Use the generic names of drugs where possible.
rules.violation_condition: using a brand name for a pharmaceutical drug instead of its generic name, or writing a generic drug name with an initial capital letter
when: Write generic names in lower case.
You can include the brand name in parentheses after the common name, using initial capitals for brand names.
rules.why: G-1, G-2, G-4: Consolidated drug naming rule with generic lower case requirement and parenthetical brand name exception.

rules.quote: When you are writing about people with a medical condition, focus on the person. Use neutral language to describe the condition. Don’t label the person.
rules.violation_condition: referring to a person with a medical condition using labelling or defining terms (e.g. 'a cancer patient', 'asthma sufferers', 'a diabetic person') rather than person-first neutral language (e.g. 'a person with cancer')
rules.why: G-1: Specific rule under the broader section on inclusive language, backed directly by Write this / Not this pairs.

examples.note: Scientific name placed in parentheses after common name

examples.note: Joined with 'or' rather than placed in parentheses

parts.quote: People with pneumonia-like infections might have Legionnaires’ disease or legionellosis.

rules.quote: If you’re writing both the scientific and common names for a medical condition, place the scientific name in parentheses. Don’t use ‘or’.
rules.violation_condition: connecting the scientific and common names for a medical condition with 'or' instead of placing the scientific name in parentheses
when: Applies when writing both the scientific and common names for a medical condition together.
rules.why: G-2: Direct rule with explicit Write this / Not this examples.
